title: The Things an Academic CV Cannot Hold
source_note: An original adaptation of the author's 2026 editorial reconstruction of 15 Pieces of Advice for Young Academics on Mental Health Day and website Film 29 synopsis; full published original not authenticated.

scenes.text: A curriculum vitae has a beautiful sense of order. Degrees, appointments, publications. The years line up neatly. The effort between those lines disappears.
A scientist can spend weeks troubleshooting an experiment. If it finally works, the finished paper receives one line. If it fails, the work may leave no line at all.
Then another deadline arrives. A report, a manuscript, a new application. The list grows while the space in which a person can rest often seems to shrink.
Rest is not the opposite of scientific seriousness. Neither is exhaustion proof of dedication. It is possible to be ambitious without treating every limit as disloyalty.
A good mentor asks difficult questions about the science, then listens to the answers. Criticism can be exacting without making humiliation part of the method.
Research protocols demand discipline, and they should. But an unhelpful result is not a verdict on the person who performed the experiment.
Sometimes the most honest laboratory note says that the expected result did not appear. That sentence can guide the next experiment, even if it cannot fill a publication list.
The academic record is rarely a photograph of the whole day. It does not show the friendships neglected, the uncertain contract, or the private conversation that made someone stay.
Some people can afford a long extension or an unpaid opportunity. Others cannot. Career choices made under different material conditions should not be mistaken for different levels of devotion.
And there must be a life that does not require an academic explanation. A conversation without networking. A meal without checking messages. An evening that belongs to nobody's evaluation.
Leaving a position can be responsible. Staying can be meaningful. What matters is whether the decision was freely made, with its costs understood rather than quietly demanded.
The CV will always be incomplete. Let it record the work. But never ask its clean columns to stand in for the whole person who did it.
